items.stem: A WHERE predicate matches about 85% of a large table, and the query needs many columns from each matching row. Which plan could reasonably be cheapest?

options.text: An index scan must be fastest because the predicate has an index.
A sequential scan may be cheaper than many index-driven row fetches.
Only the matching rows are examined, regardless of access path.

items.stem: A table has 20,000 rows. If a predicate has estimated selectivity 0.05, how many rows are estimated to pass the filter?
In one sentence, distinguish the number of rows examined during a full table scan from the number returned by a selective WHERE predicate.
Which is a real tradeoff of adding an index to a frequently updated table?

options.text: Indexes only consume storage when the indexed column contains NULL.
Indexes remove all cost from INSERT and UPDATE operations.
Indexes can improve some reads but add storage and write-maintenance overhead.

items.stem: A full table scan examines 12,000 rows and returns 300 rows. What percentage of examined rows passed the filter? Give a number from 0 to 100.
A query filters on a column with an index but the optimizer chooses a sequential scan. Give one plausible performance-based reason for that choice.
